$comment: Today's network, dated (Phase 2b.B). Hand-edited; applied at build time by pipeline/transit_pipeline/extensions.py, which cuts each stretch out of its line's GTFS geometry between two stations. A segment's 'opened' is when the track first carried passengers, from official sources only; where the track is older than today's service and its date isn't sourced, 'opened' stays null and the line's 'route_from' says when it began to use it. Schema: data/schema/extensions.schema.json.

segments.name: West Oakland to Shell Mound

sources.note: The Northern Railway: "From West Oakland to Shell Mound the road was opened August 16, 1876".

segments.notes: The Northern Railway's line north from West Oakland, opened in 1876; the Capitol Corridor's trains have run on it since 1991. Cut at today's track nearest the old Sixteenth Street station and at Shell Mound as the 1899 San Francisco sheet labels it (south of today's Emeryville station). The first biennial report's OCR reads "August 17, 1886", a misreading.

segments.name: Shell Mound to Port Costa, by Berkeley, Richmond and Pinole

sources.note: "to Martinez, January 9, 1878".
"From Shell Mound to Martinez January 9, 1878."

segments.notes: The Northern Railway's line along the bay shore to Martinez, opened in 1878. Cut at Port Costa, where trains for Sacramento took the train ferry to Benicia from 1879 to 1930; the slip as the 1898 Karquines sheet places it, on today's track.

segments.name: Port Costa to Martinez

sources.note: "to Martinez, January 9, 1878".
"From Shell Mound to Martinez January 9, 1878."

segments.notes: The Northern Railway's line to Martinez, opened in 1878.

segments.name: Martinez to Benicia, over the Martinez-Benicia bridge

sources.note: "The Martinez-Benicia bridge was opened to regular train service on October 15" (1930).

segments.notes: The Southern Pacific's bridge across Suisun Bay, which replaced the train ferry from Port Costa. The first stretch east of Martinez is the older line toward Tracy (1878), dated here with the bridge. Cut where the bridge line meets the line of 1879 from Benicia's waterfront, near Army Point.

segments.name: Benicia to Suisun-Fairfield, by Cordelia

sources.note: "to Suisun, December 28, 1879, joining there the California Pacific Railroad".
"From Benicia to Suisun December 28, 1879."

segments.notes: The Northern Railway's line from the Benicia ferry slip to Suisun, opened in 1879; today's track joins it near Army Point.

segments.name: Suisun-Fairfield to Davis, by Dixon

sources.note: The Northern Railway joined "the California Pacific Railroad" at Suisun, "forming a short line from San Francisco to Sacramento".

segments.notes: The California Pacific's line of 1868-69 from Vallejo to Sacramento. The company itself reported only that it opened "at sundry dates" in 1868 and 1869 (the tenth report, p. 63), so its date isn't sourced.

segments.name: Melrose to San Leandro, by Elmhurst

sources.note: "The last rail of the Pacific Railroad was laid on the 29th of October, in Oakland"; "On the 8th of November, the first passenger through train started from Oakland Point" (1869).
The Central Pacific's return: "To San Francisco … About December 1, 1869."

segments.notes: The Western Pacific's line of 1869 into Oakland, in the Capitol Corridor's track today (OpenHistoricalMap's tracing of the 1897 Concord sheet lies on it from Fruitvale to Elmhurst). Dated by the first through passenger train, November 8, 1869 (Halley); the railroad's own return says "about December 1, 1869". Cut at today's track nearest the end of the electric lines' Melrose segment, and at San Leandro's station as the 1948 sheet places it. Part of it, from the junction with the San Francisco & Alameda west of San Leandro, may have opened in September 1869.

segments.name: San Leandro to Niles, by Hayward

sources.note: "To Alameda Wharf September 8, 1869", by this line and the San Francisco & Alameda from San Leandro.
"the arrival there [at San Leandro] of the first train of the Western Pacific Railroad, through from Sacramento, on Monday evening, September 6th".

segments.notes: The Western Pacific's line of 1869 from Niles, opened for public use September 8, 1869 (its first train reached San Leandro on the 6th); OpenHistoricalMap's tracing of the 1899 Haywards sheet lies on today's track. Cut at Niles, where the old line went on east into Niles Canyon.

sources.note: The South Pacific Coast's return: "From Newark to Centreville February 18, 1882."

segments.notes: The South Pacific Coast's branch from Newark to Centerville, opened in 1882; OpenHistoricalMap's tracing of the 1899 Haywards sheet lies on today's track. Cut at Fremont's station, at Centerville, and where today's line meets the South Pacific Coast's main line east of Newark.

sources.note: "From Alameda Point to Los Gatos June 1, 1878", through Newark and Santa Clara.

segments.notes: The South Pacific Coast's narrow-gauge main line of 1878, later standard gauge; OpenHistoricalMap's tracings of the 1897 San Jose sheet lie on today's track, or up to about 70 m from it, as a 15-minute sheet's misregistration allows.

segments.name: Santa Clara to San José

sources.note: January 16, 1864: "The line is completed to San Jose."
"On the 16th day of January, 1864, the road was completed to San Jose, and trains commenced running to that place."

segments.notes: The San Francisco & San José's track of 1864, which Caltrain's segment dates the same way; the Capitol Corridor's trains join it west of Santa Clara's station.

sources.note: "When the Amtrak San Joaquins service was established in 1974, the ATSF line was chosen for the route"

gold-runner.notes: As the San Joaquins, renamed the Gold Runner in 2025. Amtrak's own history page with the day is offline.

sources.note: August 15, 1970: "Golden Gate Sausalito Ferry service began."
December 13, 1976: "Commute service commenced on the Larkspur route."
March 6, 2017: the district "began operating weekday commute ferry service between Tiburon and San Francisco."

1986: "Marine World established ferry service between the Ferry Building and Vallejo."

san-francisco-bay-ferry-vallejo.notes: Begun by Marine World, then run by the City of Vallejo as Vallejo BayLink, and by WETA from 2012.

sources.note: "The June 4 maiden voyage of the East Bay to South San Francisco ferry service"
January 10, 2019 "marked the launch of Richmond ferry service to San Francisco and the opening of the Richmond Ferry Terminal"
"since the route's launch on July 1, 2021."

san-francisco-bay-ferry-alameda-seaplane.notes: SF Bay Ferry's own release gives January 18, 2021, which MTC's later count contradicts.

sources.note: 2024: "launched a pilot service connecting Jack London Square to Alameda Landing"
"In 2022, Treasure Island Community Development (TICD), the master developer of Treasure Island and Yerba Buena Island, began a privately funded interim ferry service."

treasure-island-ferry-treasure-island-ye.notes: An interim, privately funded service; no official source gives the day.

sources.note: "When the AirTrain opened in 2003, we always envisioned a future project to create this extension to Long-Term Parking."

sfo-airtrain.notes: Extended to Long Term Parking in spring 2021. SFO's own releases (blocked from this build) give the dedication on March 3, 2003.

segments.name: Petaluma to Santa Rosa

sources.note: "the road to Santa Rosa was completed in October, and a passenger car at once put on the route" (p. 301); the inaugural excursion from San Francisco to Santa Rosa ran "on the last day of the year 1870" (p. 302).

The railroad's own date, "Road opened from Donahue to Santa Rosa (23 miles), January 1, 1870", which comes before the line was built (August to October 1870, Sonoma County history); the map takes October 1870.
The same January 1, 1870, as the company reported it.

segments.notes: The San Francisco & North Pacific's line of 1870; SMART has run on it since 2017. The company's own returns date it January 1, 1870, before its building in the autumn of 1870 as the county history tells it, so the map takes the history's October 1870.

segments.name: Santa Rosa to Sonoma County Airport

sources.note: "to Windsor (9 miles), March 1, 1871".
"to Windsor (9 miles) March 1, 1871".

segments.notes: The San Francisco & North Pacific's line from Santa Rosa to Windsor, opened in 1871; SMART has run on it since 2017.

segments.name: Sonoma County Airport to Windsor

sources.note: "to Windsor (9 miles), March 1, 1871".
"to Windsor (9 miles) March 1, 1871".
May 30, 2025: "Passenger service to the new Windsor station started over the weekend"

segments.notes: The San Francisco & North Pacific's line to Windsor, opened in 1871. SMART's trains reached Windsor in May 2025: MTC's post is dated Friday, May 30, 2025, so which weekend it means isn't clear; only the month is given.

segments.name: San Rafael to Petaluma

sources.note: "the Petaluma branch June 2, 1879".
"the Petaluma Branch June 2, 1879".

segments.notes: The San Francisco & North Pacific's Petaluma branch of 1879, from San Rafael; SMART has run on it since 2017. The branch met the line from Donahue at a junction near Petaluma (Poor's Manual, 1887), so the last stretch into Petaluma may be older. Through Petaluma, OpenHistoricalMap's tracing of the 1914 sheet runs up to 140 m from today's track.

segments.name: San Rafael to Larkspur

sources.note: "From San Rafael to Tiburon … May 1, 1885", opened for public use. The table's dates are printed in a column apart from its stretches and read here in order, nine dates for nine stretches; the OCR loses the running head, so the page is the research notes'.

segments.notes: The line from San Rafael to Tiburon of 1885, through the Cal Park Hill tunnel, which the San Francisco & North Pacific leased as part of its main line (the Commissioners' report, p. 16); OpenHistoricalMap's tracing of the 1897 sheet places it within about 30 m of today's track. SMART's trains reached Larkspur on December 14, 2019.

sources.note: "Since the start of service on August 25, 2017"
"SMART service began from the Santa Rosa Airport to downtown San Rafael in August 2017"

smart.notes: SMART began on August 25, 2017 between the Sonoma County Airport and San Rafael. Its track is older: the San Francisco & North Pacific's of 1870-79 and the line to Tiburon of 1885, dated here stretch by stretch for the past era, as Caltrain's is.

smart-san-rafael-larkspur.note: The Holiday Express of Saturday, December 14, 2019, "marking the official start of passenger service to the new Novato Downtown and Larkspur stations" (SMART's general manager's report, December 2019).

smart-airport-windsor.note: MTC, May 30, 2025: "Passenger service to the new Windsor station started over the weekend"; only the month is given.

sources.note: "marking the official start of passenger service to the new Novato Downtown and Larkspur stations."

SMART Novato Downtown.notes: An infill station on the 2017 line.

sources.note: January 9, 2025: the grand opening is "on Friday" (January 10).

SMART Petaluma North.notes: An infill station; MTC announced its grand opening for Friday, January 10, 2025, which isn't confirmed as the first day of service, so only the month is given.

2001: "Milpitas light rail station opens"

"The second phase, a 2.9-mile segment from I-880 to Hostetter Road", "opened for revenue service in June 2004"

segments.name: Capitol line, Hostetter Rd to Alum Rock Ave

sources.note: Where Capitol Ave crosses Alum Rock Ave.

1999: "Light rail station opens in Mountain View"
Tasman West has been in service since 1999.

Mountain View Station.notes: The end of Tasman West, which opened in December 1999 (FHWA and CPUC). Where Tasman West begins isn't named in an official source yet, so its track stays undated.

sources.note: 2005: "Winchester light rail extension opens, connecting San Jose to downtown Campbell"

Winchester Station.notes: The end of the Vasona line. Where the line leaves the Guadalupe line isn't named in an official source yet, so its track stays undated.

segments.name: San José to Gilroy

sources.note: July 1, 1992: "Service is extended to Gilroy."

segments.notes: The Southern Pacific's older line, carrying Caltrain from July 1, 1992; its own dates are for the past era. Cut at Tamien, which opened with the Gilroy service.

segments.name: 4th & King to Seventh St and 16th St

sources.note: The cutoff began "from existing tracks of the Southern Pacific in Seventh street".

segments.notes: The Southern Pacific's approach to its San Francisco terminal, older than the Bayshore Cutoff; when it first carried passengers isn't sourced. The cut is where the old line left the Seventh St tracks for Division St, as the 1950 San Francisco North sheet draws it.

segments.name: Bayshore Cutoff, Seventh St to San Bruno

sources.note: "Bay Shore Cutoff to be formally opened and in operation December 8th"
The cutoff's opening day, and "the junction with the old line at San Bruno".
"from existing tracks of the Southern Pacific in Seventh street" "to junction with the original line at San Bruno, is 9.84 miles"

segments.notes: Older than today's service, so its date is a past fact and may come from any citable source (decision 13). The San Bruno junction is where the old line meets today's track on the 1950 San Francisco South sheet.

segments.name: San Bruno to California Avenue (Mayfield)

sources.note: October 1863: "Regular service between San Francisco and Mayfield (now California Avenue in Palo Alto) begins."
"On the 17th day of October, 1863, the first train passed over the portion of the road finished, from the Mission to Big Tree Station on the San Francisquito Creek."

segments.notes: Older than today's service, so its date is a past fact and may come from any citable source (decision 13). The San Francisco & San Jose Railroad of 1863. The first train, on October 17, 1863, ran only as far as Big Tree Station on San Francisquito Creek.

segments.name: California Avenue (Mayfield) to San José

sources.note: January 16, 1864: "The line is completed to San Jose."
"On the 16th day of January, 1864, the road was completed to San Jose, and trains commenced running to that place."

segments.notes: Older than today's service, so its date is a past fact and may come from any citable source (decision 13). Cut at Polhemus Street, where the old main line into San José left it until 1935 (Southern Pacific Bulletin).

segments.name: Polhemus Street to San Carlos Street, by Diridon

sources.note: The new line follows "the existing College Park to Santa Cruz Branch" "to a point near San Carlos street".
"proceeds along the route of the Santa Cruz Branch"

segments.notes: The Santa Cruz branch's older track, which the main line took over on December 31, 1935; when it first carried passengers isn't sourced. The San Carlos St cut is where the 1943 San Jose sheet draws the new line leaving the branch.

segments.name: San Carlos Street to Tamien: the line of 1935

sources.note: "The new line was opened to traffic at 12:01 a.m., December 31."
December 1935: "A new terminal opens on Cahill Street in San Jose".
"Southerly from San Carlos street an entirely new line is to be constructed on private right-of-way, joining the existing main line near Lick Station".

segments.notes: Older than today's service, so its date is a past fact and may come from any citable source (decision 13). The new line ran on to the main line at Lick, south of Tamien; that part is in the Gilroy stretch.

caltrain-san-jose-gilroy.note: "Service is extended to Gilroy" on July 1, 1992 (Caltrain milestones, 1990s).

caltrain.notes: Dated from July 1, 1980, when Caltrans took over the Peninsula Commute Service; the trains before then are the past era's Southern Pacific Peninsula line, on the same track. The track itself is dated stretch by stretch, from the San Francisco & San Jose Railroad of 1863-64, the Bayshore Cutoff of 1907 and San José's line of 1935.

sources.note: July 1, 1980: "The new agreement takes effect, with Caltrans assuming responsibility for the Peninsula Commute Service."
June 23, 1975: "Fourth and Townsend streets terminal opens in San Francisco."

Caltrain 4th & King.notes: Today's San Francisco terminal, at Fourth and Townsend Sts.

sources.note: July 1, 1992: "Tamien station opens in San Jose."
December 1935: "A new terminal opens on Cahill Street in San Jose, now known as San Jose Diridon Station."
